gloss: Concerned with beauty, artistic effect, or appearance.
Beautiful or appealing to one's sense of beauty or art.
The study of art or beauty.
That which appeals to the senses.
The set of artistic motifs defining a collection of things, especially works of art; more broadly, their aura or “vibe”.
An archipelago of Italy, off the north coast of Sicily, comprising seven significant islands: Lipari, Vulcano, Salina, Stromboli, Filicudi, Alicudi and Panarea.
Living or taking place in the air.
Made up of air or gas; gaseous.
Positioned high up; elevated.
Ethereal, insubstantial.
A rod, wire, or other structure for receiving or transmitting radio, television signals etc.
A move, as in dancing or skateboarding, involving one or both feet leaving the ground.
A move that involves performing a full rotation while in the air, without touching any equipment such as a balance beam or panel mat with one's hands.
An aerial photograph.
air or aircraft
A Trojan hero and the legendary ancestor of Romans.
A male given name from Ancient Greek.

A mythological shield associated with the Greek deities Zeus and Athena (and their Roman counterparts Jupiter and Minerva) shown as a short cloak made of goatskin worn on the shoulders, more as an emblem of power and protection than a military shield. The aegis of Athena or Minerva is usually shown with a border of snakes and with the head of Medusa in the center.
Guidance, protection; endorsement, sponsorship.
The study or philosophy of beauty.
An artist's principles, preferences, and/or his agenda
A mixture of fine solid particles or liquid droplets suspended in a gaseous medium.
An aerosol can.
The payload (e.g. insecticide, paint, oil, cosmetics) and propellant contained by an aerosol can.
A colloidal system in which the dispersed phase is composed of either solid or liquid particles and in which the dispersal medium is some gas, usually air.
The practice of flying maneuvers involving aircraft attitudes that are not used in conventional passenger-carrying flights.
Living or occurring only in the presence of oxygen e.g. aerobic bacteria.
Of exercise, performed while maintaining a sufficient supply of oxygen to meet bodily energy needs.
Of or relating to aerobics.
An airfield.
Any area of land or water used for aircraft operation, regardless of facilities.
An airfield used for managed aircraft operation, either military or civilian, having such facilities as are necessary for operation.
An airfield equipped with air traffic control facilities and hangars as well as accommodation for passengers and cargo; an airport.
The science of the dynamics of bodies moving relative to gases, especially the interaction of moving objects with the atmosphere.
The aerodynamic properties of a particular object (typically a car or aircraft).
The design, construction, mathematics, and mechanics of aircraft and other flying objects; the study of and control of how aviation works.
The theory and practice of aircraft navigation.
Someone who cultivates an unusually high sensitivity to beauty, as in art or nature, often in a manner perceived to prioritize beauty over other qualities such as virtue and utility.
The establishment of a cause, origin, or reason for something.
The study of causes or causation.
The study or investigation of the causes of disease; a scientific explanation for the origin of a disease.
A cause of disease or of any particular case of a disease (but see pathology § Usage notes).
The activity or technique of photographing the surface of the Earth from an aircraft, rocket, etc.
Photographs taken by this means, collectively.
An aircraft, such as a dirigible or balloon, that derives its lift from buoyancy rather than from wings or rotors.
A moored balloon flown in a semi-permanent manner, such as a border patrol monitoring balloon affixed at 18,000 feet (~6 km).
The swallowing of air, especially in hysteria.
A certificate indicating that a student is ill, excusing attendance at lectures and examinations and allowing courses to be passed without finishing the work.
An unclassified degree awarded to such a student.
The production of weather charts.
A branch of surrealist art in which a three-dimensional object is used as a stencil.
the study of gases in equilibrium and of balloons or aircraft in varying atmospheric conditions
The study of the dispersion of airborne biological materials, as pollen, spores, microorganisms, or viruses.
The branch of meteorology involving the observation of the atmosphere by means of balloons, kites, rockets, drones, airplanes, etc.
The study of the air and of the atmosphere and technological methods involved.
A sea in the northeastern part of the Mediterranean.
A form of exercise, designed to enhance one's cardiovascular fitness, normally performed to music.
A wireless message.
A telegram whose transmission included at least one segment sent via airplane.
A thin piece of foldable and gummed paper for writing a letter and serving as its own envelope for transit via airmail.
A pneumogram.
A Greek dramatic poet (525 BCE—456 BCE); Aeschylus was the earliest of the three greatest Greek tragedians.
A male given name from Ancient Greek.
A mechanically-extendable ladder mounted to a fire engine.
An elected official who was responsible for the maintenance of public buildings, regulation of festivals, supervision of markets and the supply of grain and water.
A state of inactivity and metabolic depression during summer: the summer version of hibernation.
The arrangement (vernation) of the parts of a flower inside a bud; prefloration.
The spending or passing of a summer.
A porous, ultralight solid-state substance, similar to gel, in which the liquid component is replaced with gas.

A steam engine powered by rocket propulsion due to escaping steam, consisting of a pressure vessel mounted on a bearing, with one or more tubes which exhaust steam tangentially to the rotation axis so as to create rotation, which is mostly regarded as a curiosity with no practical use.
A meteorite consisting of silicate minerals.
To supply with oxygen or air.
To bubble or sparge with a gas, especially oxygen or air.
To incorporate a gas, especially oxygen or air, into a solid or semisolid material.
In an aesthetic manner; with a pleasing sensory effect.
A telekinetic ability to control the movement of air.
The study of pollen grains and spores (palynomorphs) in the atmosphere.
Of, or relating to the Earth's atmosphere and nearby space.
Of, or relating to the science, technology and industry associated with aircraft, missiles, satellites and spacecraft.
Of or relating to the Aegean Sea or the regions bordering it.
Of or relating to the Bronze Age civilization in that region.
Having to do with aerial navigation
A person who travels through the air in an airship or balloon.
Having to do with acrobatic maneuvers, such as spins, twirls, and flips, performed by an airplane.
A male given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage.
The process by which air is circulated through or mixed with a substance such as soil or a liquid.

By extension, a process in which other gases (such as carbon dioxide or nitrogen or argon) are circulated through or mixed with a substance (usually liquid), sometimes with the consequence of increasing the transfer of air into the same liquid at the surface due to the induced circulation.
A device which mixes air with a substance, particularly soil or a liquid.
A device used for charging mineral waters with gas and in making soda water.
A fumigator used to bleach grain, destroying fungi and insects.
A doctrine which holds aesthetics or beauty as the highest ideal or most basic standard.
An instrument used to measure the mass and density of gases.
of, or relating to the wind.
carried, deposited or eroded by the wind.
Aeolian mode
The scientific study of the effect of aerodynamic loads on structures.
The effect of aerodynamic load on a given structure.
The god of medicine and healing. Greek counterpart: Asclepius.
A heavier-than-air aircraft, deriving its lift from motion.
An open box over which strings are stretched that sound when the wind passes over them.
A canister whose pressurized contents may be released as an aerosol when a button is pressed.

Any musical instrument which produces sound primarily by causing a body of air to vibrate, without the use of strings or membranes, and without the vibration of the instrument itself adding considerably to the sound.
A form of combined speaking trumpet and ear trumpet.

An instrument for greatly intensifying speech, consisting of a phonograph diaphragm arranged so that its action opens and closes valves, producing synchronous air blasts sufficient to operate a larger diaphragm with greater amplitude of vibration.
Divination by use of atmospheric conditions.
A goat-like creature resembling a satyr, sometimes portrayed as having a fish's tail.
A classic epic poem, written in Latin by Virgil in the 1st century BCE (between 29 and 19 BCE), that tells the legendary story of Aeneas fleeing Troy and settling in Italy as ancestor of the Romans.
A person who studies aerodynamics.
A spongy, airy tissue found especially in the roots of aquatic plants.
The ability to perceive sensations.
Any form of life that is sustained by the presence of air (or oxygen)
An Ancient Greek author, famous for the fables ascribed to him.
A mountainous region of Greece on the north coast of the Gulf of Corinth, forming the eastern part of the modern prefecture of Aetolia-Acarnania.
The name of a number of characters in Greek mythology, including the founder of the Aeolian race, and a god with power over wind.
A practitioner of aeromancy.
Of or relating to Aesculapius, the Greco-Roman god of medicine.
Medical, concerning healing.
A device used to collect dust particles, spores etc from the air for subsequent analysis.
A type of compressed air camera for making films, constructed by Polish inventor Kazimierz Prószyński in 1909
Movement of an organism either towards or away from a region of higher oxygen content.
The growth of an organism either towards, or away from a region of higher oxygen content.
Of or pertaining to aeroelasticity
The office of an aedile.
The period or duration of this office.
Of or relating to Aeschylus, an ancient Greek dramatic poet.
A train that is supported on a cushion of air, in the manner of a hovercraft.
A nymph of the island that bears her name.
91 Aegina, a main belt asteroid.
An island of Greece.
An inhabitant of Aegina.
Any member of the genus Aeonium of succulent, subtropical plants with rosette leaves on a basal stem, mostly native to the Canary Islands.
Of or pertaining to aerospace.
The mythical island said to be the home of the sorceress Circe.
A character in the founding myth of Athens.

that moves both on sea and in the air
A mode whose scale is the same as a natural minor scale, with the interval pattern
A surgeon who performs aesthetic surgery
Synonym of eternity (“existence without end”).
Synonym of aevum (“the temporal mode of existence between time and eternity, said to be experienced by angels, saints, and celestial bodies (which medieval astronomy believed to be unchanging)”).
The science of measuring the air, including air pressure, density, quality, direction and condensation; pneumatics.
Of or relating to that ancient people who resided in Italy.
A member of the Aequi.
The Italic language spoken by the Aequi.
A maker of model aircraft.
Relating to the transmission of energy via pressurised air
One of the Greek primordial deities who was the personification of light, brother-husband of Hemera and grandson of Chaos.
Of or relating to Aetolia.
A native or inhabitant of Aetolia.
A subdivision of the Silurian period.
An Italic tribe of northeast Latium and the central Apennines of Italy who appear in the early history of ancient Rome.
Relating to the heating of surfaces due to their contact with the flow of air or other gases
A transliteration of the Ancient Greek male given name Ἀέτιος (Aétios), Aetius.
A male given name in Latin, Aetius.
The goddess/personification of good health and the glow of health, one of the daughters of Asclepius.
96 Aegle, one of the main belt asteroids.
A thin fabric resembling crape
A mechanical device used to provide temporary access to areas at high levels.
The condition of having an aerodynamic shape
A European species of nonvenomous snake, Zamenis longissimus, associated with Asclepius (Roman counterpart: Aesculapius) in Ancient Greek mythology.

Colored foam that streams out of a spray can, as a party favor; a ropey emission of this foam.

A celebrated Greek statesman and orator (389–314 B.C.E.; full name Αἰσχίνης Ἀτρομήτου Κοθωκίδης, Aeschines Atrometi f. Cothocides), one the Canon of Ten Attic Orators.
Synonym of Cataeschinians
Of or relating to the mythical island of Aeaea.
A king of the island of Aegina in the Saronic Gulf, one of the three judges in Hades.
A prefecture (nome) in the west of Greece.
A group of islands in the Aegean Sea.

A son of King Priam, either by the naiad Alexirrhoë or the seer Arisbe, who interpreted the dreams of Queen Hecuba when she bore Paris and who mourned the deceased daughter (either Asterope and Hesperia) of the river-god Cebren; in Ovid’s Metamorphoses transformed by Tethys (Cebren’s mother) into a diving seabird (perhaps a cormorant or Scopoli’s shearwater) when he threw himself from atop a sea-cliff in grief.
A daughter of Poseidon and the Pleiad Alcyone, daughter of Atlas. She was loved by Apollo and bore to him Eleuther and Linus.
Former name of Linosa (“Mediterranean island”).

A king of Colchis, son of Helios and Perseis.
